# Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials {#sec-cases}



The earlier chapters argued in general terms: that a Bayesian rule monitored continuously can reach the same conclusion as a fixed design with fewer events, that the saving comes from the monitoring and not from a lower bar, and that every gain has a price. This chapter tests the argument on five trials that were actually run, and it keeps the argument honest by choosing them to differ. SELECT is the favorable case: a large effect, cleanly estimated, in a trial big enough for the asymptotics to apply. REWIND is the unfavorable case: an effect half as large on the log scale, which barely cleared its threshold and in which the scheduled design wins. SURPASS-CVOT is an active-comparator case with a noninferiority margin, where the lesson is what the margin and a transportability assumption allow a Bayesian reading to say. TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 is a different kind of case: a trial with two prespecified design features, a biomarker-guided treatment duration and baseline tau strata, that a Bayesian analysis could be proposed to handle differently. BNT162b2, the last case, is a trial that was Bayesian in its confirmatory analysis as well as in its design, and that led to an emergency use authorization and a biologics license.

Each case follows the same order, in line with the rule of this book that the traditional design comes first. We say what the trial did and how it was monitored; we then reconstruct the Bayesian alternative on the trial's own published numbers; and we close with what a data monitoring committee (DMC) and a regulator would have had to accept in order to act on it. Everything in the SELECT and REWIND reconstructions and in the stratum illustration for TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 is a counterfactual, and we say so each time it matters. BNT162b2 is the exception: its Bayesian analysis was the trial's actual analysis. No sponsor ran these trials the way we simulate them, and nothing here is a claim that any of them should have stopped early. The reconstructions are a way of pricing the design choices in units that a sponsor, a payer and a regulator can all read: events, patients, years, quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and money.

::: {.callout-important title="Regulatory anchor"}
The governing texts for this chapter are the ones that decide whether a monitoring rule is acceptable, not the ones that decide whether a drug is. Status as of November 2026.

- **ICH E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials** (Step 4, 5 February 1998), Section 4.5: "all interim analyses should be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol." A rule that looks at the data repeatedly is an interim-analysis plan, Specify the monitoring plan prospectively. E9 permits justified amendments before unblinded access to comparative data, with their statistical consequences addressed. Section 3.4 names group sequential designs as the usual way to look repeatedly.
- **FDA, Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics** (final, November 2019), Section III: the chance of erroneous conclusions should be adequately controlled, treatment-effect estimates should be sufficiently reliable, design details should be completely prespecified, and trial integrity should be maintained. Section VI.A: simulations are the way to estimate operating characteristics. These four principles are the test every reconstruction below has to pass.
- **FDA, Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products** (draft, January 2026), Section IV.A: the draft describes three routes for Bayesian success criteria. One is calibration to a type I error rate: for trials with an overall frequentist statistical analysis plan the draft says criteria are "almost always" chosen so that the familywise type I error is no greater than 0.025 one-sided, and a criterion of the form $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c$ can have $a$ and $c$ chosen so that this holds (Section IV.A.1 uses $a = 0$ for calibrated superiority designs). The others are direct interpretation of posterior probabilities, for example with borrowing and by agreement with FDA, and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria (Section IV.A.3). Calibration is this book's default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing, and the route this chapter follows; it is one of FDA's routes and not its universal requirement, and a draft recommends and does not require. The prior must be prespecified (Sections IV.B and V).
- **FDA, Demonstrating Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness** (revised draft, June 2026): the statutory standard of adequate and well-controlled investigations, and the conditions under which one trial with confirmatory evidence can suffice. Cardiovascular outcomes trials are usually the only large trial a sponsor has, which makes this the standard in play.
- **FDA, Diabetes Mellitus: Evaluating Cardiovascular Risk in New Antidiabetic Therapies to Treat Type 2 Diabetes** (final guidance, December 2008; withdrawn in March 2020, when FDA issued the draft guidance "Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Evaluating the Safety of New Drugs for Improving Glycemic Control", which remains a draft), which asked sponsors of new type 2 diabetes drugs for cardiovascular safety evidence, in practice a comparison of the upper bound of the 95 percent confidence interval for the cardiovascular risk ratio against margins of 1.8 (to support approval) and 1.3 (to be shown, if the premarketing bound lies between the two, by a postmarketing trial) [@fda2008diabetescv]. This guidance is the setting of REWIND. SELECT enrolled people without diabetes and is not governed by them.

None of these documents requires or forbids what is reconstructed here. The chapter's position is that the reconstructions would have to satisfy these texts, and it checks them one by one at the end of each case. See @sec-regulatory for the full map, @sec-sequential for group sequential boundaries, @sec-evalues for e-values and @sec-simulation for the simulation report.
:::

## SELECT: semaglutide and cardiovascular events {#sec-cases-select}

### The trial as conducted

SELECT randomized 17,604 adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease, without diabetes, to weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo, at 804 sites in 41 countries, enrolling from 2018 to 2021 [@lincoff2023semaglutide]. The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke, analyzed as time to first event. It occurred in 569 of 8,803 patients on semaglutide and 701 of 8,801 on placebo: 1,270 events in all, hazard ratio 0.80 with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.72 to 0.90, and $p < 0.001$. Mean follow-up was 39.8 months.

This is the traditional trial in its standard form: an event-driven design with a single primary hypothesis, a Cox model for the hazard ratio, an independent DMC, and a final analysis at which the type I error is spent. SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83 (a 17 percent reduction) with 90 percent power at one-sided 0.025, which calls for 1,225 planned events, and it planned one superiority interim analysis at two thirds of the planned events (about 817) followed by the final analysis, with the group sequential design accounted for in the final test [@ryan2020select]. The textbook formula at the design hazard ratio gives about 1,211 events, close to the plan. The observed hazard ratio of 0.80 was more favorable than the design alternative. The four-look O'Brien-Fleming design below is a separate hypothetical comparator, and SELECT's actual two-look design is carried through every comparison as a fourth rule. The reconstruction asks a different question from the one the sponsor faced: if the true hazard ratio were 0.80 and the trial's information as observed, what would each monitoring scheme, each held to the same one-sided error of 2.5 percent, have needed?

In information time the trial is a clean object. With $d = 1{,}270$ events, the standard error of the log hazard ratio is approximately $2/\sqrt{d}$, because each event carries about $1/4$ of a unit of Fisher information under 1:1 allocation (this is the standard approximation for a log-rank or Cox analysis, and it is why $I_n = d/4$ throughout this chapter). The log hazard ratio is $\theta = -\log(0.80) = 0.2231$ in the book's sign convention, so that benefit is positive, and the final standardized score is $Z = 3.98$.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
d_tot <- select_design$d_tot; HR <- select_design$HR; tau <- select_design$tau
theta <- -log(HR); se <- 2 / sqrt(d_tot)
z_final <- theta / se
```
:::


The published interval implies a standard error of 0.0569 against our 0.0561, so this parametrization reproduces the trial to two digits. That is all the model has to do: it is a summary of how information accrued, not a model of the disease.

### Three monitoring schemes and SELECT's own design, one error rate

A speed comparison means nothing unless the rules carry the same type I error under the monitoring each actually uses, and this is where naive comparisons fail. We compare three rules and add SELECT's actual design as a comparator.

1. **Group sequential, O'Brien-Fleming.** Four equally spaced looks at 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent of the events, with the O'Brien-Fleming boundaries on the $Z$ scale of 4.049, 2.863, 2.337 and 2.024 (see @sec-sequential; the working paper printed 4.05, 2.87, 2.34 and 2.03 from a rounded constant; the reconstruction uses the exact values above). It can act only at a scheduled look. This is the design most event-driven outcomes trials use today, and it is the one a regulator will expect to see first.
2. **Bayesian posterior probability, monitored on a fine event grid.** Stop for benefit when $\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid \text{data}) \ge p^\ast$, with a normal prior on the log hazard ratio centered at zero with scale $\tau = 0.25$ (a prior 95 percent interval for the hazard ratio of 0.61 to 1.63, a skeptical prior in the sense of @sec-priors), and $p^\ast$ chosen so that the one-sided type I error is 2.5 percent when the rule is evaluated at every second event from 4 to 1,270. The simulator monitors on this grid and to this horizon, not literally continuously, and "continuous" below means this grid. This is the criterion $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c$ of the FDA draft, with $a = 0$ and $c = p^\ast$.
3. **E-value mixture, monitored on the same grid.** Stop for benefit when the mixture e-value reaches $1/\alpha = 40$ (see @sec-evalues). By Ville's inequality, this cannot have a type I error above 2.5 percent however often it is looked at, and in practice it realizes less.
4. **SELECT's actual design (comparator).** One superiority interim at two thirds of the 1,225 planned events (817) and a final analysis at 1,225, with Lan-DeMets O'Brien-Fleming-type spending of the one-sided 0.025 at the planned interim, as in the SELECT statistical analysis plan (section 2.1, Table 2-1: nominal one-sided levels of about 0.00605 at the interim and 0.02314 at the final). Its boundaries on the $Z$ scale are reported with the results below. We do not calibrate it; we report its realized error. Crossing the boundary is necessary but not sufficient for stopping: at the actual interim, at 831 events, the efficacy boundary was crossed and the data monitoring committee recommended continuing (FDA clinical review of NDA 215256 s011, pp. 65-66).

The Bayesian and e-value rules use the same normal prior with the same scale and are functions of the same score; the Bayesian rule thresholds the posterior probability of benefit, the e-value rule the mixture likelihood ratio. Because the Bayesian rule's type I error is calibrated by simulation, it is acceptable under the calibration route of the FDA draft: the posterior is the way the decision is expressed, and the frequentist operating characteristics are the way it is justified.

The simulation below uses `select_simulate()` from the companion package, which ports the code of the working paper. It generates 40,000 event-time score paths on the grid of every second event (plus 817, 1,225 and 1,270) with the hazard ratio held at the observed 0.80 for the power calculation and at 1.0 for the type I error, evaluates each rule on the same paths, and calibrates $p^\ast$ as the empirical $1-\alpha$ quantile of the maximum of the posterior probability along each null path.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" cache.extra='79fbd08d7b14b2cd023ca719e6a37655'}

```{.r .cell-code}
res <- select_simulate(nsim = 40000, seed = 31415)
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center" cache.extra='79fbd08d7b14b2cd023ca719e6a37655'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Independent check of the calibrated threshold: 40,000 fresh null score paths (a different seed) on the same event grid.
set.seed(2718)
I_g <- res$dg / 4; A_g <- I_g + 1 / tau^2; dI <- diff(c(0, I_g)); K <- length(I_g)
hit <- 0; nval <- 40000
for (b in 1:10) {
  S <- t(apply(matrix(rnorm(4000 * K, sd = rep(sqrt(dI), each = 4000)), 4000), 1, cumsum))
  hit <- hit + sum(apply(pnorm(sweep(S, 2, sqrt(A_g), "/")), 1, max) >= res$pstar)
}
val_typeI <- hit / nval; se_mc <- sqrt(0.025 * 0.975 / nval)
```
:::




A posterior probability rule at the conventional threshold of 0.975, monitored on the same grid, has a type I error of about 11.8 percent rather than 2.5. That is the phenomenon of a repeated-significance test (@sec-sequential) in a different notation. Any claim that a Bayesian rule decides sooner at the conventional threshold is an artifact unless the error is reported with it. The calibrated threshold is 0.9952. Selecting an empirical null quantile fixes the rejection proportion in the calibration sample at 2.5 percent; it does not make the population error exactly 2.5 percent. With 40,000 paths the binomial standard error near 0.025 is about \ensuremath{8\times 10^{-4}}. On 40,000 fresh null paths with a different seed the calibrated threshold rejects in 2.68 percent, which is 0.18 points from 2.5 percent, or 1.6 standard errors of the difference between two independent estimates of that precision. The realized error of the calibrated rule is therefore known only to within a few tenths of a point, which is why the calibration and its validation should use more paths than a protocol-stage sketch needs. A protocol would repeat the validation, and the calibration, across its nuisance scenarios (event rate, accrual, nonproportional hazards). The e-value rule realizes well under its 2.5 percent budget, in our run 0.58 percent, because Ville's inequality protects against every stopping time and this trial uses only a few of them; Polson and Sokolov report 0.55 percent in their run of the same design, and the two differ by less than two Monte Carlo standard errors [@polson2026bayesstandard]. The four-look O'Brien-Fleming design realizes about 2.55 percent because its looks are discrete, and SELECT's actual design 2.54 percent; both agree with 2.5 percent within Monte Carlo error. The comparator's boundaries are 2.51 at 817 events and 1.99 at 1,225 on the $Z$ scale.

The headline numbers are in @tbl-select, and every stopping time is stated with its conditioning. Among simulated trials that declare efficacy, the median stopping point is 464 events for the Bayesian rule, 612 for the e-value rule and 952 for the four-look O'Brien-Fleming design. Over all simulated trials, counting a trial that never crosses as ending at its maximum, the medians are 486, 714 and 952. The all-trial figures are the fairer basis for comparing rules of different power: the e-value rule reaches its bar in only 83 percent of replications even at full information, so its conditional median describes only the trials that succeed, and its all-trial median is 47 percent above the Bayesian rule's (32 percent on the conditional scale). Power is 94.7 percent for the Bayesian rule, 83.1 for the e-value rule and 97.7 for the four-look design. SELECT's actual two-look design stops at a median of 817 events (it ends at 1,225 if it never crosses), with power 97.4 percent and realized type I error 2.54 percent. Against that actual design the Bayesian rule's all-trial median is 41 percent lower, with 2.7 points less power. The four-look design, at 952, is later than SELECT's actual design for two reasons: it cannot act between looks, and its early boundaries are very high. Crossing the first interim boundary of 4.05 would need the equivalent of about 1,300 events at this effect size, more than the trial ever accrued, so the first interim analysis of such a design is, on the mean path, arithmetically incapable of stopping this trial (about 2 percent of simulated paths cross 4.05 at that look). The conditional medians (464, 612, 952) are close to the working paper's 464, 608 and 952 [@polson2026bayesstandard]; the R random stream differs from the Python stream used there, and every simulated number in this book is the R one.

:::::

The two group sequential designs have the highest power in the table (97.7 and 97.4 percent), and the reason is instructive: they spend their error budget where the information is, and do not need to protect against stopping times they never use. The Bayesian rule is faster and has a little less power (94.7 percent). That trade is the price of monitoring on a fine grid, so the table is a trade and not a ranking. A sponsor who will in fact look only a few times has no reason to buy protection for looking at every second event.

@fig-select-bars shows the same story on the scale a DMC works on. On the mean path the statistic $Z$ grows like $\sqrt{d}$, and each rule is a curve (or four points) that the statistic has to cross.

The group sequential rules have far fewer moments at which noise can help them.

In our run the Bayesian conditional median ranges from 462 to 494 events and the all-trial median from 494 to 510, and the e-value conditional median from 594 to 674 and its all-trial median from 710 to 766, with power as shown. The ranges differ slightly from those in the working paper, which are for a different random stream; the ordering does not. The point estimate of a trial that succeeded is on average somewhat optimistic, so a trial run at the true effect would, to that extent, need more events than these medians, and this reconstruction is not a power calculation made before the trial. It is a description of what each rule needs to see if the world is as the trial found it.

### What the saving would be worth in calendar time and exposure

From here to the end of the chapter every conversion of events into time, exposure, QALYs or money is a modeled counterfactual: it combines the simulated stopping distribution with an accrual model and with assumptions about what would have happened to patients after a decision. Translating events into calendar time needs an accrual model. We take enrollment linear over 36 months, the trial running to 60 months, and events accruing in proportion to cumulative person time, which reproduces a mean follow-up of 42 months against the reported 39.8.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m <- select_month_of_events(c(Bayes = mda_b, `e-value` = mda_e, `O'Brien-Fleming` = mda_o, `SELECT actual` = mda_a), d_tot)
m_b <- m[["Bayes"]]
```
:::


The all-trial median decision points fall at month 34 for the Bayesian rule, month 41.6 for the e-value rule, month 49.5 for the four-look group sequential design and month 45 for SELECT's actual design, against a read-out at month 60. The Bayesian median falls about 8 months before the e-value median, 15 months before the four-look design's, 11 months before SELECT's actual design's, and 2.2 years before the trial's read-out.

The quantity that matters clinically is exposure. Total exposure in SELECT was about 58,400 patient-years (enrollment times the reported mean follow-up of 39.8 months), of which about 29,200 were on placebo. The accounting below (@tbl-worth-exposure) converts the expected stopping point of the Bayesian rule, averaged over all simulated trials with the trials that never cross counted at their maximum, into the placebo patient-years and placebo events that would come after it. Three assumptions carry it: events are uniform in person time, placebo participants would have been offered active treatment at the decision so that the events they would otherwise have had are prevented at the trial's observed relative reduction, and the decision would have been acted on. The figures are an order of magnitude and not a count. For REWIND the median follow-up of 5.4 years stands in for the mean, and the two are not the same.

### What the monitoring committee would have seen

The medians in @tbl-select are a summary. The question a DMC faces is concrete: at this look, with these data, does the rule permit a recommendation? @tbl-looks answers it on the mean path at the four looks a group sequential design would have scheduled.

Two readings of the table should be separated. At the first interim, the group sequential committee is shown a standardized score of 1.99 against a boundary of 4.05 and must continue. The Bayesian committee is shown a posterior probability of benefit of 96.5 percent and must also continue, since its calibrated threshold is 99.5 percent. The two agree. At the second interim they part. The score is 2.81 against a boundary of 2.86, so the four-look design continues by a margin of 0.05; the e-value stands at $\log E = 2.4$ against the 3.69 it needs; and the posterior probability of benefit is 99.63 percent, which clears the calibrated threshold, so the Bayesian rule stops. On the mean path, the four-look design stops at the third look, another 317 events after the Bayesian decision at the second look.

The near miss at the second look is a reminder of how much turns on the spacing of looks, which a group sequential design fixes in advance. The calibrated Bayesian rule may act at any count on its prespecified monitoring grid, within the 1,270-event horizon. It is also a reminder of why a mean path is not a trial: a single real path would sit above or below 2.81 at that look, and the four-look rule would have stopped on a substantial fraction of paths there. SELECT's actual interim, at 817 events, would show a mean-path score of 3.19 against a boundary of 2.51, but the trial's actual interim came at 831 events, where the efficacy boundary was crossed and the data monitoring committee recommended continuing (FDA clinical review of NDA 215256 s011, pp. 65-66). Crossing is necessary but not sufficient for stopping, which is one more reason to read the reconstruction through the all-trial table and not through the mean path.

::: {.callout-note title="Technical note: why the e-value rule is slow here" collapse="true"}


The e-value rule uses the same normal prior scale $\tau$ and the same score $S$ as the Bayesian rule, with $I_n = d/4$ events-based information and $A = I_n + 1/\tau^2$. The simulated Bayesian rule acts when $\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid \text{data}) = \Phi(S/\sqrt{A}) \ge p^\ast$, which on the scale $Z = S/\sqrt{I_n}$ is $Z \ge \sqrt{1 + 1/(I_n\tau^2)}\, z_{p^\ast}$ with $z_{p^\ast} = \Phi^{-1}(p^\ast)$, or $Z^2 \ge (1 + 1/(I_n\tau^2))\, z_{p^\ast}^2$ with $Z > 0$. The e-value rule acts when the mixture likelihood ratio $E_n$ reaches $1/\alpha$, which on the same scale is $Z^2 \ge (1 + 1/(I_n\tau^2))\,[\log(1 + I_n\tau^2) + 2\log(1/\alpha)]$ with $Z > 0$. At $\tau = 0.25$ and $p^\ast = 0.9952$ the Bayes bar is $Z^2 \ge 7.6$ at 464 events and 7.0 at 1,270, and the e-value bar is 10.8 and 10.9, so the e-value rule asks for 3.2 more units of $Z^2$ at 464 events and 3.9 more at 1,270. The constant $2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38$ at $\alpha = 0.025$ is, for this normal-mixture construction and in the large-information approximation, the surcharge of the e-value bar over the uncalibrated Bayes-factor rule at posterior odds 1, $Z^2 \ge \log(1 + I_n\tau^2)$, of @sec-sequential and @sec-evalues; the exact surcharge is $7.38\,(1 + 1/(I_n\tau^2))$. It is not a universal cost of anytime validity, since other e-processes behave differently. It is also not the surcharge over the calibrated posterior-probability rule simulated here, whose bar $p^\ast$ was itself raised by simulation to pay for monitoring on the grid. The e-value rule's realized type I error of about 0.6 percent against a budget of 2.5 percent is the visible form of the remaining difference: it is paying for protection at stopping times this trial never used. In this construction the surcharge is a constant in the large-information approximation, and its relative cost falls only as $1/\log I_n$; see @sec-evalues.
:::

### What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept

The reconstruction is only useful if the Bayesian rule could have been proposed, accepted and run. Walk through the four principles of the FDA adaptive-designs guidance [@fda2019adaptive] and the success-criterion language of the Bayesian draft [@fda_bayesian_2026].

*Error control.* This is met by construction in the reconstruction, on the event grid and to the 1,270-event horizon, because $p^\ast$ was found by simulation so that the one-sided familywise type I error under the monitoring plan is 2.5 percent. That fixes the rejection proportion in the calibration sample, not the population error, so a protocol would report the Monte Carlo uncertainty (about 0.0008 at 40,000 paths), validate the threshold on independent null simulations as above, and repeat both across nuisance scenarios. The draft describes calibration as one of three routes, and for a design with a frequentist analysis plan and no borrowing it is the usual one. The weakness is that the calibration holds under a specific monitoring plan. A rule calibrated to a fine grid is conservative for a DMC that meets twice a year, because any subset of the grid inherits the bound. A rule calibrated to meetings twice a year is anti-conservative if the committee also looks ad hoc, for example after a safety signal. A DMC that cannot commit to a schedule can calibrate to a dense grid at the cost of a higher threshold, but monitoring off the grid or beyond the horizon needs recalibration, and a trial that cannot bound its looks should use a fixed design, a spending function or an anytime-valid rule.

*Reliable estimation.* A trial that stops at the conditional median of 464 events yields a hazard ratio estimate that is biased away from the null on average, as is true of trials that stop early for efficacy, and the confidence interval is wider than the interval from 1,270 events by about $\sqrt{1270/464} = 1.65$. The Bayesian posterior shrinks the estimate towards the prior, which is a correction in the right direction but not a free one. The trial's other jobs would also suffer: the key secondary endpoints, the safety database for an agent intended for long-term use, and the subgroup results a label depends on all need events and patient-years, not just a primary endpoint that crossed a bar. For a drug intended for chronic use by people without diabetes, a regulator may well prefer the longer exposure. This is a real cost and the reason the calendar saving in this chapter should not be read as a recommendation.

*Prespecification.* The prior scale, the threshold, the monitoring schedule and the stopping rule would all have to be written into the protocol and the statistical analysis plan, prospectively. E9 requires interim analyses to be planned and described in the protocol (Section 4.5) and permits justified amendments before unblinded access to comparative data, with their statistical consequences addressed [@ich_e9]. The simulation report that supports them is the operating-characteristics evidence the FDA asks for (@sec-simulation).

*Trial integrity.* The DMC would have been shown a posterior probability and a threshold instead of a boundary. The sponsor would remain blind to the interim comparisons, as it does under a group sequential plan. Nothing about the Bayesian rule changes the firewall; what changes is the number the committee reads.

The regulator's question about the prior is the one a group sequential design never faces. Here it is answered the way the draft asks: the prior is skeptical, it is prespecified, and its influence on the decision is bounded by the calibration, since a different $\tau$ changes $p^\ast$ and leaves the simulated type I error unchanged (see @sec-priors). A regulator who accepts that the final decision rule is "reject when the calibrated posterior probability exceeds $p^\ast$" is accepting a test with simulated size and power, which is also what it accepts from an O'Brien-Fleming design. In the language of the substantial-evidence draft [@fda_single_trial_2026], the evidence in either case is a single well-controlled trial whose persuasiveness comes from its effect size and its error control, and a hazard ratio of 0.80 with a final score near 4 is persuasive under any of the rules.

## REWIND: where the scheduled design wins {#sec-cases-rewind}

### The trial as conducted

REWIND randomized 9,901 patients with type 2 diabetes to weekly dulaglutide or placebo, enrolling from August 2011 to August 2013 with a median follow-up of 5.4 years, and reported in 2019 [@gerstein2019dulaglutide]. The primary composite cardiovascular outcome occurred in 594 of 4,949 on dulaglutide and 663 of 4,952 on placebo, so 1,257 events, with a hazard ratio of 0.88, a 95 percent interval from 0.79 to 0.99, and $p = 0.026$.

REWIND ran in the regulatory setting of the 2008 diabetes guidance [@fda2008diabetescv], which asked sponsors of new glucose-lowering drugs to show that the drug did not raise cardiovascular risk beyond a prespecified margin on the hazard ratio. That is the historical context, but REWIND itself was designed to demonstrate cardiovascular superiority, with 90 percent power, and not merely to exclude the 2008 margin [@gerstein2019dulaglutide]. A reconstruction that asks about stopping for benefit is therefore as natural for REWIND as for SELECT, and the contrast below is about the size of the effect and not about the purpose of the trial.

The information content is almost identical to SELECT, 1,257 events against 1,270. The effect is half the size on the log scale, 0.128 against 0.223, so the final standardized score implied by the rounded hazard ratio is 2.27 rather than 3.98 (2.23 is implied by the published two-sided $p$ value of 0.026; the gap is rounding in the hazard ratio). This is a trial that barely cleared its threshold, and it is exactly the case in which the advantages of continuous monitoring should be expected to shrink.

### What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept

The honest conclusion for REWIND is that the scheduled design was the right choice, and a Bayesian statistician advising the sponsor would have said so if the expected effect was a hazard ratio near 0.88. Four things follow for a protocol.

First, the reconstruction does not rescue the argument for continuous monitoring in a marginal trial, and it should not be offered to a regulator as if it did. The regulator's concern with a glucose-lowering drug would also include the one stated in the 2008 guidance: precision at the upper bound of the interval, which is a property of the full trial and cannot be got from half of it.

Second, the same Bayesian machinery is useful for a different purpose in such a trial. A posterior distribution for the hazard ratio from the final data, with a skeptical prior, answers the question the 2008 guidance asks (is the upper bound of the effect on cardiovascular risk below the margin?) in the units of the margin. This does not change when the trial can stop; it changes how the result is reported (@sec-bayes and @sec-evidence).

Third, the contrast between SELECT and REWIND is itself the finding. The saving from continuous Bayesian monitoring grows with the size of the effect relative to the precision, which a sponsor knows only roughly in advance. The assurance calculation of @sec-power is the tool for deciding which design to pick before the trial: the average of the probability of success over a prior on the effect. A prior that puts most of its mass on hazard ratios near 0.80 favors continuous monitoring; a prior centered at 0.90 does not.

Fourth, the reconstruction conditions on the observed effect. For REWIND this is a hazard ratio of 0.88 that barely cleared the bar. Had the true effect been closer to 0.90 the trial would more likely have failed, and the reconstruction would show fewer simulated trials declaring efficacy at a true hazard ratio of 0.90. Assessing early futility would require an additional prespecified rule and a separate operating-characteristics calculation (@sec-predictive).

## SURPASS-CVOT: an active comparator and a noninferiority margin {#sec-cases-surpass}

The preceding two cases compared a drug with placebo. SURPASS-CVOT compared two active drugs, which changes the question [@nicholls2025surpasscvot]. It randomized 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, double blind and 1:1, to weekly tirzepatide (up to 15 mg) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg, the dose that REWIND had shown to reduce cardiovascular events. After 134 exclusions for ineligibility the modified intention-to-treat population was 13,165 (6,586 on tirzepatide and 6,579 on dulaglutide). The primary outcome was the first of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke, and the primary hypothesis was noninferiority: the upper limit of the 95.3 percent confidence interval for the hazard ratio had to lie below 1.05, and superiority could be claimed if the upper limit was below 1.00. The traditional logic of the noninferiority test, a margin fixed in advance and a one-sided bound on the interval, is the one set out in @sec-testing.

The primary outcome occurred in 801 patients (12.2 percent) on tirzepatide and 862 (13.1 percent) on dulaglutide, a hazard ratio of 0.92 with a 95.3 percent confidence interval from 0.83 to 1.01. Noninferiority was established ($p = 0.003$) and superiority was not ($p = 0.09$). We omit the secondary and component hazard ratios, which we have not checked against the full report.

The posterior probability that tirzepatide is noninferior, that is, that the hazard ratio is below 1.05, is 0.996, and the probability that it is superior is 0.954. The trial "failed" to show superiority because the upper limit of 1.01 sat just above 1.00, yet the probability that the hazard ratio is below one is 0.95. These are not competing statements: the frequentist $p = 0.09$ is the chance, if the hazard ratio were exactly one, of data at least this extreme in either direction, and the posterior probability is a statement about the hazard ratio given the data and a flat prior. Neither is wrong, and a decision-maker needs the second to weigh a benefit against a cost. The probability of a reduction of at least 10 percent is only 0.33, which is the honest size of the uncertainty about how much better tirzepatide is. The assumption of transportability from REWIND is the whole of the argument, and it is exactly what a Bayesian borrowing model makes explicit and discounts. The calculation, the discounted versions and the comparison with the published indirect analysis of @sattar2026imputed are in @sec-borrowing-chain; the clinical point is that two numbers for the same question differ in what they adjust for, and an indirect comparison rests on its assumptions.

## TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2: a prespecified biomarker strategy and baseline tau strata {#sec-cases-alz}

### The trial as conducted

TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 randomized 1,736 participants with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease to donanemab or placebo, with efficacy measured at 18 months (76 weeks), and reported a 35 percent slowing of decline on its integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale (iADRS) in the prespecified low and medium tau population of 1,182 participants, and a 22 percent slowing in the combined population of 1,736 [@sims2023donanemab]. The primary analysis was prespecified for two populations, the tau-defined one and the combined one, and the trial therefore had to choose how to spend its type I error between them. The order of testing is given in the publication and its supplement [@sims2023donanemab].

This is a traditional design in the sense of this book: a fixed duration, a prespecified primary analysis with a multiplicity procedure across populations, and a single final analysis. It differs from a textbook parallel-group trial in two respects. Both are prespecified design features, and neither is Bayesian as conducted; a Bayesian analysis could be proposed for the second.

### Two prespecified design features

The first is that treatment duration was guided by a biomarker. Participants completed their course of donanemab once they reached a prespecified level of amyloid plaque clearance, and the report gives 52 percent of the low and medium tau participants as having reached the clearance criterion by one year, among those with a PET assessment at that visit [@sims2023donanemab]. This is a stopping rule applied to each participant rather than to the trial, driven by an intermediate biomarker. It is a prespecified biomarker-guided treatment strategy, and it does not require Bayesian inference. It is related to individualized dosing in the patient-specific dose-finding designs reviewed in @sec-dose, and because it depends only on each participant's own biomarker and not on accumulating comparative results, it is a treatment strategy and not a trial adaptation in the sense of the FDA guidance. It is also a rule that a fixed-duration comparison cannot evaluate on its own: the trial estimates the effect of the strategy "stop when cleared" against placebo, not the effect of a fixed dose and duration, and the estimand has to say so (ICH E9(R1), @sec-randomization).

The second is baseline tau stratification. The trial reports a 35 percent effect in one stratum and a 22 percent effect in the combined population. Tau status is measured at baseline, and the strata do not change in response to accumulating results, so this is baseline stratification and not an adaptive feature. The standard apparatus requires that the populations and the order of testing be designated before the data arrive, and the designation then governs the claim. A prespecified hierarchical model (@sec-borrowing, @sec-multiplicity) could estimate effects in both disjoint strata with borrowing between them. Population claims and their success criteria would still require prespecification and an evaluation of false-positive risks. The sizes of the two strata, 1,182 participants in the low and medium tau stratum and 552 in the high tau stratum as reported, do not by themselves establish that borrowing would be large; that depends on the between-stratum variance, as the illustration below shows.

The arithmetic of that shrinkage is simple enough to show. Suppose the two strata have estimated effects with standard errors proportional to $1/\sqrt{n}$, and the between-stratum standard deviation $\tau_b$ of the true effect is the quantity the data cannot tell us much about. The weight on the stratum's own estimate is $\tau_b^2/(\tau_b^2 + s^2)$, where $s$ is its standard error and $\tau_b$ is the between-stratum standard deviation. The smaller the stratum and the smaller the between-stratum variance, the more the estimate is pulled to the pooled one.

### What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept

Which analysis a regulator prefers is not a question we can settle. The trial as conducted had to choose a primary population and a multiplicity procedure, and it did, in a way the FDA could review against the substantial-evidence standard. A hierarchical Bayesian analysis of the two strata would be a proposed alternative, not a description of what the trial did, and would need three things the draft guidance asks of any borrowing: a prespecified model, a stated rationale for exchangeability of the strata, and a simulation of its type I error across the scenarios in which the effect is present in one stratum only (@sec-borrowing). Those scenarios are the ones that matter, because a hierarchical model that shrinks a null stratum towards a positive pooled effect will raise the false-positive rate for that stratum. The regulatory cost is a longer simulation report and a more demanding conversation about the prior on the between-stratum variance.

For the biomarker-guided duration, the regulator's concern is the estimand and the integrity of blinding (the blind has to survive the switch when a participant stops active treatment after clearance, which is a matter of masking procedure and not of the analysis). Neither is Bayesian or frequentist. They are the design properties that made a prespecified biomarker-guided feature acceptable to the FDA in this case.

The lesson is different from SELECT's. In SELECT, a Bayesian monitoring rule would change when the trial stops. In TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2, the traditional apparatus handled two prespecified features, and the trial shows that regulators accept them when they are specified in advance. A hierarchical Bayesian analysis of the strata would not make the trial more or less adaptive. It would express the stratum analysis through one model in place of a testing hierarchy, at the price of the prespecification and simulation described above.

## BNT162b2: a Bayesian confirmatory trial that led to an authorization {#sec-cases-bnt}

### The trial as conducted

The phase 2/3 trial of the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine (Protocol C4591001, Pfizer and BioNTech) began in July 2020 and reported the efficacy of the vaccine in preventing COVID-19 [@polack2020bnt]. Its statistical analysis plan, posted on ClinicalTrials.gov, makes the primary analysis Bayesian [@pfizer_sap_2020]. This case differs from the other four in kind: the Bayesian rule is not a counterfactual reconstruction but the decision rule the trial itself used, and it supported a regulatory action. The beta-binomial model of @sec-bayes is the whole of the machinery.

### The Bayesian element

The conjugate beta-binomial model, with prior Beta(0.700102, 1) on the vaccine share of cases, the transformation to VE and the posterior arithmetic, is worked in full in @sec-bayes-practice. The plan calls the prior minimally informative and says it can be considered pessimistic. The case-specific points are the success criterion, $\Pr(\mathrm{VE} \ge 30\% \mid \text{data})$, which must exceed 0.995 at an interim analysis and 0.986 at the final analysis, with the thresholds calibrated so that the overall one-sided type I error is 2.5 percent (Section 7.1 of the plan; the calibration is the kind of simulation of @sec-simulation). Two primary objectives, VE in participants with no evidence of prior infection and VE in all participants, were evaluated in sequence. The final analysis was planned at 164 first primary cases, with interim looks and a futility rule based on the predictive probability of success, nonbinding, of 5 percent or less.

Two features set it apart from SELECT's reconstruction. The bar is on VE of 30 percent, a margin of clinical relevance, and not on zero, so the criterion is the $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c$ of the FDA draft with $a$ different from zero. And the model is conjugate, so each look is a closed-form calculation with no simulation of the posterior itself, only of the operating characteristics.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
a0 <- 0.700102; pi30 <- 0.7 / 1.7              # VE = 30% corresponds to pi_v = 0.7/1.7
pr_ve30 <- function(v, p) pbeta(pi30, a0 + v, 1 + p)   # v vaccine cases, p placebo cases
th <- qbeta(c(0.975, 0.5, 0.025), a0 + 8, 1 + 162)
ve <- round(100 * (1 - (2.222 / 2.214) * th / (1 - th)), 1)   # posterior 2.5%, 50%, 97.5% for VE; surveillance-time ratio 2.222/2.214 (FDA briefing, Table 6)
```
:::


### What happened and what the regulator did

The published analysis counted 8 cases in the vaccine group and 162 in the placebo group, a vaccine efficacy of 95.0 percent with a 95 percent credible interval of 90.3 to 97.6 percent [@polack2020bnt]. Our calculation (@sec-bayes-practice), with the surveillance-time ratio of 2.222 to 2.214 reported in the FDA briefing document, gives 90.3 to 97.6 percent against the published 90.3 to 97.6 (the counts of 8 and 162 are exact), and a posterior probability of VE above 30 percent that is indistinguishable from one (1), far above 0.986. FDA issued an emergency use authorization on 11 December 2020 for individuals 16 years of age and older [@fda_eua_pfizer_2021], and approved the biologics license application (Comirnaty) on 23 August 2021, again for those 16 and older [@fda2021comirnaty].

### The lesson for this chapter

Where the SELECT and REWIND reconstructions are counterfactuals, BNT162b2 shows the regulatory path already traveled: a minimally informative prior, a margin, calibration to 0.025 one-sided, and a protocol that fixed the thresholds before the first case. One caution. The plan on ClinicalTrials.gov is a sponsor document with several amendments. The efficacy boundaries tabulated in the plan, written as case splits, reproduce from the stated prior: at the final analysis of 164 cases, 53 vaccine cases is the largest count with $\Pr(\mathrm{VE} > 30\% \mid \text{data}) > 0.986$ (53 gives 0.990, 54 gives 0.985). The backing for a rule of this kind comes from @sec-bayes for the model and @sec-simulation for the calibration.

## What the saving is worth {#sec-cases-worth}

A claim that a design decides at 486 events (the all-trial median; 464 among trials that declare efficacy) rather than 1,270 is not yet an argument that anyone outside the field will weigh. This section converts it into five currencies. Every conversion is a modeled counterfactual, and the conversions differ in how many assumptions they stack. They use the expected stopping point over all simulated trials, so that trials which never cross, and therefore save nothing, are counted.

### Inside the trial: events and QALYs

These figures are modeled counterfactuals: arithmetic on the trial's own counts and the simulated all-trial stopping distribution, under the assumptions stated above (events uniform in person time, placebo participants switched at the decision, the decision acted on).

Uniform event rates in person time and a switch of placebo participants at the decision are assumed. REWIND person-time uses the median follow-up as a stand-in for the mean.'}

x$share <- x$d_dec / x$d_tot                       # expected share of events accrued at the Bayesian decision

### Trial cost

Moore and colleagues reviewed the pivotal trials of 59 novel agents approved by the FDA in 2015 and 2016 [@moore_pivotal_costs_2018]. The median estimated cost of a pivotal trial was \$19.0 million, the costliest single trial in the review was about \$347 million, and the mean estimated cost of the five cardiovascular pivotal trials was \$157.2 million (their Table 2). SELECT, with 17,604 patients at 804 sites in 41 countries and about five years of follow-up, is far larger than the typical trial in that review, and we have no published cost for it. We therefore take the cited cardiovascular mean of \$157 million as the base case and \$350 million and \$600 million as scenarios for a larger trial, not as estimates of the cost of any particular trial.

The saving is not proportional to the whole budget. Variable costs, which are site payments, patient visits, monitoring, laboratory work and drug supply, scale with person-time; fixed costs, which are protocol development, startup, regulatory work and the final analysis, do not. With 56.5 percent of the person-time avoided on average, the modeled saving is that share of the variable share.

### Timeline and the acceleration bound

Under the accrual model above, the all-trial median Bayesian decision falls at month 34 against a read-out at month 60, so 26 months or 2.2 years earlier. ### Label revenue brought forward



The largest sum in the accounting is commercial, and it rests on the least. Patent expiry is fixed, so a cardiovascular indication reached earlier adds the same number of years of protected, label-driven sales. Novo Nordisk reported global Wegovy sales of DKK 58.2 billion for 2024 [@novo_annual_report_2024]. The share of sales that the cardiovascular label drives is not public, and we assume 10 to 25 percent. At an assumed 6.9 DKK per dollar the 2024 sales are about \$8.4 billion, and brought forward by the all-trial median saving of 2.2 years the label-driven revenue is \$1.8 billion to \$4.6 billion. This is a modeled counterfactual of revenue, not profit, and an upper bound: approval, reimbursement and uptake would not all have moved forward by the full statistical acceleration, for the reasons given for the population bound above, and the sales level, the label share and the exchange rate are assumptions.

REWIND gives the same arithmetic only conditionally. Trulicity (dulaglutide) had revenue of \$4.13 billion in 2019 [@lilly_form10k_2021], and the FDA approved its cardiovascular indication on 21 February 2020 [@fda_trulicity_cv_letter_2020]. In the reconstruction the Bayesian rule acts in only 49 percent of simulated REWIND trials, so the all-trial median saving is zero, because fewer than half of the simulated trials cross. The unconditional expected saving can still be positive: the mean decision falls at 973 of 1,257 events, so on average 23 percent of the events and person time would come after it. The revenue figures below describe the conditional median among trials that cross, and multiplying the crossing probability by a conditional median would not give an expected revenue (that needs the calendar saving averaged over all paths, which the summary output does not keep). Conditional on its acting, the median decision falls at 680 of 1,257 events. Under an accrual model with an assumed 24 months of linear enrollment and the 85 months between the registered start and primary completion dates [@ctgov_rewind_2019], that is month 51, or 2.8 years before the read-out. With an assumed 10 to 20 percent of 2019 sales attributable to the label, the revenue brought forward would be \$1.2 billion to \$2.3 billion, but only in the trials in which the rule acts, and the scheduled design acts more often there.

Two caveats from the earlier sections apply to every currency in this section. Among trials stopping early for efficacy, naive estimates tend to exaggerate benefit. Skeptical priors may reduce this bias; bias and interval coverage should be evaluated for the specified estimator and stopping rule. And a regulator would want safety follow-up to continue after an efficacy decision, which recovers only part of the cost saving.

## Side by side: what changes in the protocol {#sec-cases-side}

| | Traditional (what the trials did) | Bayesian reconstruction | What the regulator will ask |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Monitoring | Event-driven; DMC reviews at scheduled looks, boundaries from a spending function (SELECT: one interim at two thirds of the planned events) | Monitoring of a posterior probability on a fine event grid | The monitoring plan, written in advance (E9 4.5) |
| Decision rule | Test statistic crosses a boundary | $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > p^\ast$ | Calibration of $p^\ast$ to 0.025 one-sided by simulation, with Monte Carlo error |
| Type I error | Spent by alpha spending | Calibrated by simulation under the plan | Simulation report, scenarios, Monte Carlo error |
| Prior | None | Skeptical normal on the log hazard ratio | Prespecified, with sensitivity to $\tau$ |
| Where it wins | Marginal effects, fixed looks (REWIND) | Large effects, DMC that can commit to a plan (SELECT) | Evidence the choice was made before the data |
| What does not change | Randomization, blinding, endpoint, firewall, intention-to-treat estimand | Same | Same |

Where the two agree numerically: with a flat prior, the posterior probability of benefit equals one minus the one-sided $p$ value, so a single-look Bayesian rule with threshold $c$ is the fixed one-sided test at level $1 - c$.

### What a Lp(a)HORIZON result does to OCEAN(a)

When an analyst moves the probability that a related trial succeeds from $p_0$ to $p_1$ after a sibling reads out, the analyst has implicitly applied a Bayes factor, the ratio of the posterior odds to the prior odds:

$$B = \frac{p_1/(1 - p_1)}{p_0/(1 - p_0)}.$$

We could not confirm a published analyst estimate of the probability of success of OCEAN(a)-Outcomes after the Lp(a)HORIZON announcement of 4 September 2026, so we use an illustrative move from 50 to 20 percent, which is not a finding about any analyst.



On that illustration $B = 0.25$: the analyst treats the Lp(a)HORIZON result as 4 times as likely if olpasiran fails as if it succeeds. A fall from 50 percent to 40, 30 or 10 percent implies factors of 0.67, 0.43 and 0.11. Whether the factor is reasonable depends on how much the two drugs share, which the announcement does not settle: it reports that Lp(a) was lowered and that the primary endpoint was not met, with no hazard ratio and no comparison with the depth of lowering of other agents [@novartis_horizon_2026]. That is the information set of the September announcement. The full results of 7 November 2026 reported a hazard ratio of 1.02 (95 percent interval 0.90 to 1.15) overall and 1.00 (0.87 to 1.15) among patients with Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL, with Lp(a) at 12 months of 64.4 nmol/L on pelacarsen against 233.4 on placebo, a difference of 72 percent [@cho2026pelacarsen]. On the flat-prior normal approximation to the log hazard ratio, the posterior probability that the hazard ratio is below 0.90 is 0.023, below 0.85 0.002 and below 0.80 0.0001, so a 10 percent or larger benefit is largely ruled out for pelacarsen at its depth of lowering. These are the sizes of benefit compatible with HORIZON, and they inform OCEAN(a) only to the extent that olpasiran's benefit is expected to track that of pelacarsen. If the benefit of Lp(a) lowering is proportional to the absolute reduction, a drug that lowers it further should be judged against a different benchmark and the factor should be closer to 1. A hierarchical model with the depth of lowering as a covariate makes that assumption explicit and lets the data weigh it, which one revised probability does not.

## Limits of the reconstruction {#sec-cases-limits}

The numbers above are order-of-magnitude arguments, and a reader should know exactly where they would break.

- **The counterfactual is not the trial.** The Bayesian rule is evaluated on simulated paths with the observed hazard ratio. Nobody observed a SELECT that stopped at 486 events, and the conditional medians describe only the paths that crossed, which are the lucky ones.
- **Calibration is under a known grid and horizon.** A threshold of 0.9952 is calibrated for evaluation at every second event up to 1,270 events, not for literally continuous monitoring. Any subset of that grid, including unscheduled meetings at event counts on it, inherits the error bound, because the maximum over a subset cannot exceed the maximum over the grid. Monitoring off the grid or beyond the horizon needs additional justification and a recalibration, and the calibration is a property of the plan and not of the number.
- **The error rates are estimates.** A type I error read from 40,000 paths has a Monte Carlo standard error of about 0.0008, and the calibrated threshold should be validated on independent null simulations and across nuisance scenarios.
- **The information model is approximate.** The calculation assumes a Gaussian score process with $I_n = d/4$, proportional hazards and 1:1 allocation, which is accurate to two digits for the final analysis and approximate for early looks.
- **Early stopping costs something not priced here.** The secondary endpoints, safety exposure, subgroup results and the label depend on events and time, and a regulator weighs them.
- **The economic figures are scenarios.** The QALY value per event, the variable cost share and the access counterfactual are assumptions that a reader can vary and should.
- **Selection.** SELECT and REWIND are trials that were published. The fixed hazard ratio is the successful trial's own estimate.

::: {.callout-tip title="In the protocol"}
Language a sponsor could use if it chose the Bayesian monitoring rule for an outcomes trial: "The DMC will review unblinded efficacy data at each scheduled meeting, at most twice a year. At each review the trial may be stopped for efficacy if the posterior probability that the hazard ratio is below 1 exceeds 0.9952 under a normal prior on the log hazard ratio with mean zero and standard deviation 0.25. The threshold was calibrated by simulation (Appendix X) on a grid of event counts, every second event up to 1,270 events, so that the one-sided familywise type I error is estimated at 0.025 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.0008) and was confirmed on independent null simulations. A review at any event count on the grid, including a meeting not on the schedule above, is covered by that calibration. A review beyond 1,270 events or at an event count off the grid is not covered, requires a protocol amendment and a recalibration, and the simulation report gives the operating characteristics for hazard ratios from 0.70 to 1.00 and a range of event rates." The values are those of this chapter's reconstruction, not a recommendation for any particular trial.
:::

## Key points {.unnumbered}

- Using a common nominal one-sided bound of 2.5 percent (the Bayesian rule is calibrated to it by simulation, the four-look design by its boundaries, and the e-value rule is controlled by its bound through Ville's inequality), a Bayesian rule monitored on a fine event grid stops, among simulated trials that declare efficacy, at a median of 464 events on SELECT's data, against 612 for an e-value rule and 952 for a four-look O'Brien-Fleming design. Over all trials, counting those that never cross at the 1,270-event read-out, the medians are 486, 714 and 952, with power 95, 83 and 98 percent and realized type I errors of 2.5, 0.58 and 2.55 percent. SELECT's actual two-look design (one interim at two thirds of 1,225 planned events) stops at a median of 817 with power 97 percent and realized type I error 2.5 percent; the trial reported at 1,270. This is a reconstruction that uses the trial's observed hazard ratio and is not a power calculation.
- An uncalibrated posterior threshold of 0.975 on the same grid has a type I error of about 12 percent. Any claim of speed has to come with the error it was calibrated to, and with the power.
- On REWIND, where the hazard ratio is 0.88 and the final score is 2.27, the advantage shrinks: the Bayesian rule declares efficacy in only 49 percent of runs, so its all-trial median is the maximum of 1,257 events (680 among the trials that succeed), and the four-look design has the highest power. Monitoring on a fine grid is expensive when the effect is marginal.
- SURPASS-CVOT shows what a Bayesian reading adds to a noninferiority trial: posterior probabilities of noninferiority, of superiority and of a clinically meaningful reduction on a continuous scale, and an indirect comparison with placebo whose transportability assumption has to be stated and can be discounted.
- TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 shows that regulators accept a prespecified biomarker-guided treatment strategy and a prespecified two-population analysis with baseline tau strata when the rules are written in advance. A hierarchical Bayesian analysis of the strata is a proposed alternative that would itself need prespecification and a simulation of its false-positive risk.
- Unlike the counterfactual reconstructions above, BNT162b2 is a Bayesian confirmatory trial whose actual analysis supported an EUA and a BLA: a prespecified beta-binomial posterior, a bar set on vaccine efficacy of 30 percent and not on zero, and thresholds calibrated to a one-sided type I error of 2.5 percent.
- The in-trial value of the SELECT saving is, as a modeled counterfactual, of order a hundred QALYs (112 to 224 under stated assumptions) and tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, computed from the all-trial stopping distribution; the population-level value is orders of magnitude larger but is a bound, not a forecast.
- The label-driven revenue that an earlier SELECT decision would have brought forward is, as a modeled counterfactual, of order a few billion dollars of Wegovy revenue (\$1.8 billion to \$4.6 billion under an assumed label share of 10 to 25 percent), an upper bound and not profit. The REWIND analogue holds only conditionally on the Bayesian rule acting.
- Trials still running show where the same ideas apply now: a discounted prior from a sibling trial, a predictive interim, and a hierarchical model across a drug class. The TRIUMPH-3 posterior depends on the prior, with the probability of some benefit between 0.72 and 1.00 across the priors considered, and none of the rows is a confirmatory result.
- A calibration is a property of the monitoring plan, its event grid and its horizon, and it is estimated with Monte Carlo error. The reconstruction is a counterfactual, and no part of it argues that these trials should have stopped early.
